Apophis: The Asteroid That’s (Almost) In Trouble

Normally, when an asteroid swings by Earth, the burning question is simple: “Are we at risk?” Should we prepare for a massive space rock to pancake our planet? Not this time. In the case of Apophis, the 400-meter-wide asteroid that’s due to zip past us in April 2029, the tables are turned entirely.

According to a study published in The Planetary Science Journal, it’s the asteroid itself that could run into some serious trouble during its flyby. When Apophis makes its close approach—coming within just 32,000 kilometers (that’s about 20,000 miles!) from Earth—it’s more than far enough for us humans to sleep easy. But it’s close enough for Apophis to experience some cosmic consequences.

When Gravity Has a Bone to Pick

First things first: as Apophis nears Earth, our planet’s gravity is going to put on a little show. Earth’s gravitational pull won’t reel the asteroid in like a fishing rod, but it will tug and twist at Apophis just enough to potentially alter its rotation, tweak its orbit, or even cause mini-landslides and cracks across its surface. This is a known phenomenon called tidal effects—it’s what happens when a massive body (in this case, Earth) passes close by another, stirring up some mayhem as it goes.

While this isn’t great news for Apophis, for scientists it’s an extraordinary opportunity. When asteroids like Apophis are shaken up by tidal forces, their inner secrets—usually hidden beneath the surface—can get exposed to our watchful instruments. Imagine a cosmic piñata breaking open, revealing clues about the asteroid’s structure and makeup. It’s similar to what happens to comets when they approach the Sun: the heat melts ice and releases the hidden particles inside.

Space Traffic and the (Very Slight) Risk Factor

But wait—there’s another cosmic twist. What if Apophis collided with a piece of space debris? Geostationary satellites, which orbit at about 36,000 kilometers above Earth, could—hypothetically—find themselves on a collision course with the asteroid. Now, don’t picture the sky packed with SpaceX constellations; most satellites at that altitude are dedicated to weather forecasting or telecommunications, and there are only about 600 of them in active service.

Throw in a handful of stray space debris (whose numbers at this altitude are, let’s admit, anyone’s guess), and the possibility of a collision becomes a worrying, if remote, prospect.

Yet, after crunching the numbers, the authors of the study concluded that… everything should be just fine! The risk of a collision is actually extremely low. However, if an accident did happen, all subsequent plans for observing Apophis could be turned upside down, as its trajectory might be altered in totally unpredictable ways.

The Science Race Is On

This challenge is even more important since the European Space Agency (ESA) is rallying its resources to track Apophis during its close approach—and in the aftermath—thanks to the Ramses mission. Ramses follows on the heels of the successful Hera spacecraft launch, continuing the agency’s dedication to planetary defense and scientific study. Set for launch in April 2028, Ramses will play a crucial role during Apophis’s flyby in April 2029, coming closer to Earth than most interplanetary guests would ever dare.

Meanwhile, NASA’s Osiris-Apex probe is racing toward the same goal. Both Ramses and Osiris-Apex could find their work seriously complicated—or even rendered useless—if Apophis’s path is thrown off course by a freak encounter with a piece of debris.

The fate of the Ramses mission itself will depend on upcoming decisions in November at the ESA Ministerial Council. The good news? Japan’s likely participation could be just what’s needed to convince all ESA member countries to give the mission the final green light.

So, while Apophis’s visit has us safe and sound, it’s the asteroid—and the ambitious fleet of probes racing to study it—that are walking the cosmic tightrope. Stay tuned and keep your telescopes handy: 2029 might just be the year when the universe reminds us how lively our solar system really is!
